title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 2, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 16–17 (Night 228, continuing nights-227), transcribed from the scan (archive.org aliflailaorbook02unkngoog) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 228 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. Bound and beaten in the fire-worshippers' underground chamber, al-Asʿad remembers the glory and kingship he has lost and laments in verse. He eats a little of the loaf and drinks a little of the salt water left by his head, and lies awake all night for the bugs and lice. In the morning the slave-girl changes his clothes, and his skin, stuck to the shirt with blood, comes away with it; he cries out to God that he will bear it if it pleases Him, and asks Him to take his due from those who wronged him, in two poems of patience. The slave-girl beats him again until he faints and leaves him alone in chains, bleeding and far from those he loves, weeping for his brother — and morning overtakes Shahrazād. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الثَّامِنَةُ وَالْعِشْرُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَتَيْنِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-thāminatu wa-al-ʿishrūna baʿda al-miʾatayni
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the eighth and the twenty after the two-hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the two hundred and twenty-eighth night,
sentences.n: The night's opening formula: the unit, al-thāminatu, comes before the tens and is joined to them by wa-, all in the nominative with al-laylatu. The ئ of المائتين is printed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ الْأَسْعَدَ لَمَّا رَأَى نَفْسَهُ مُقَيَّدًا مَضْرُوبًا وَقَدْ آلَمَهُ الضَّرْبُ تَذَكَّرَ مَا كَانَ فِيهِ مِنَ الْعِزِّ وَالسَّعَادَةِ وَالْمُلْكِ وَالسِّيَادَةِ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-Asʿada lammā raʾā nafsahu muqayyadan maḍrūban wa-qad ālamahu al-ḍarbu tadhakkara mā kāna fīhi mina al-ʿizzi wa-al-saʿādati wa-al-mulki wa-al-siyādati
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that al-Asʿad, when he-saw himself fettered, beaten, and-the-beating had pained-him, remembered what he-was in-it of the-might and-the-happiness, and-the-kingship and-the-lordship.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that when al-Asʿad saw himself fettered and beaten, and the beating had left him in pain, he called to mind the honour and happiness, the royalty and command that had once been his.
sentences.n: The night opens by retelling the last words of the night before. anna al-Asʿada lammā …, “that al-Asʿad, when …”: the subject of anna is put first, and the clause with lammā comes between it and its verb, tadhakkara. nafsahu, “his self”, is the ordinary Arabic for “himself”. wa-qad ālamahu, “the beating having pained him”: wa- with qad and a past verb gives a circumstance already complete. The sajʿ falls again on al-saʿāda / al-siyāda. The hamza of رأى, the madda of آلمه and the shadda of تذكّر and of العزّ are printed.

sentences.t: فَبَكَى وَصَعَّدَ الزَّفَرَاتِ وَأَنْشَدَ هٰذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ
sentences.tr: fa-bakā wa-ṣaʿʿada al-zafarāti wa-anshada hādhihi al-abyāta
sentences.l: And-he-wept, and-sent-up the-sighs, and-recited these verses:
sentences.i: He wept and heaved deep sighs, and recited these lines:
sentences.n: ṣaʿʿada, Form II of ṣ-ʿ-d, “to make rise”: with zafarāt, “sighs”, it is “to heave sighs”, the sighs rising from the breast. anshada, Form IV of n-sh-d, “to recite verse”. abyāt, plural of bayt, “a line of verse”.

sentences.t:
قِفُوا بِرُسُومِ الدَّارِ وَاسْتَخْبِرُوا عَنَّا * وَلَا تَحْسِبُونَا فِى الدِّيَارِ كَمَا كُنَّا
لَقَدْ فَرَّقَ الدَّهْرُ الْمُشَتِّتُ شَمْلَنَا * وَمَا تَشْتَفِي أَكْبَادُ حُسَّادِنَا مِنَّا
تَوَلَّتْ عَذَابِي بِالسِّيَاطِ لَئِيمَةٌ * وَقَدْ مَلَأَتْ مِنِّي جَوَانِحُهَا ضِغْنَا
عَسَى وَلَعَلَّ اللهُ يَجْمَعُ شَمْلَنَا * وَيَدْفَعُ بِالتَّنْكِيلِ أَعْدَاءَنَا عَنَّا
sentences.tr:
qifū bi-rusūmi al-dāri wa-istakhbirū ʿannā * wa-lā taḥsibūnā fī al-diyāri kamā kunnā
laqad farraqa al-dahru al-mushattitu shamlanā * wa-mā tashtafī akbādu ḥussādinā minnā
tawallat ʿadhābī bi-al-siyāṭi laʾīmatun * wa-qad malaʾat minnī jawāniḥuhā ḍighnā
ʿasā wa-laʿalla Allāhu yajmaʿu shamlanā * wa-yadfaʿu bi-al-tankīli aʿdāʾanā ʿannā
sentences.l:
Halt at (the) traces (of) the-abode and-ask-for-news about-us, * and-do-not reckon-us in the-dwellings as we-were.
Indeed has-split the-fate, the-scatterer, our-gathered-union, * and-not are-healed (the) livers (of) our-envious-ones of-us.
Has-taken-charge-of my-torment with-the-whips a-base-woman, * and-filled against-me (have) her-ribs (with) rancour.
Maybe, and-it-may-be, God gathers our-union * and-drives-off with-the-making-an-example our-enemies from-us.
sentences.i:
Stop at the traces of our home and ask what became of us, * and do not think to find us in that land as once we were.
Fate, the great divider, has broken up our company, * and still the hearts of those who envy us have not had their fill of us.
A base woman has taken my torment in hand with her whips, * and her breast is full of spite against me.
Yet perhaps, it may be, God will bring us together again, * and drive our enemies from us and make an example of them.
sentences.n: Four lines in the metre ṭawīl, rhyming in -nā. The print points the verse fully. Line 1 opens with the oldest move in Arabic poetry, the halt at the rusūm, “traces”, of an abandoned dwelling; istakhbara ʿan, Form X of kh-b-r, “to ask for news of”: ʿan marks the one asked about. lā taḥsibūnā, “do not reckon us”, prohibition with the jussive, taḥsibū, and the object -nā. shaml, “a gathering, the state of being together”: farraqa shamlahum, “he broke up their union”, is a fixed phrase, and al-mushattit, “the scatterer”, from Form II of sh-t-t, repeats the idea. tashtafī, Form VIII of sh-f-y, “to be healed”, used of rancour that is “cured” by revenge; the akbād, “livers”, plural of kabid, are the seat of hatred and grief, as the heart is in English; min marks the one revenge is taken on. tawallā, Form V of w-l-y, “to take charge of”, the very verb of the old man's order the night before. laʾīma, “a base, mean woman”, is the slave-girl. jawāniḥ, plural of jāniḥa, “the ribs about the breast”, so “her breast”; ḍighnā, “rancour”, is an accusative of specification, “filled in respect of spite”, held in pause at the rhyme. ʿasā and laʿalla both mean “perhaps”, set side by side for emphasis. After laʿalla Classical Arabic puts its noun in the accusative, Allāha; the print points اللهُ with a damma, Allāhu, as if ʿasā governed it; the metre is the same either way, and the damma is kept. tankīl, verbal noun of Form II of n-k-l, “to make an example of by punishment”: bi- of means. The print writes the hamza on أَكْبَادُ, لَئِيمَةٌ, مَلَأَتْ and أَعْدَاءَنَا, writes Allāh without its shadda, اللهُ, and spells fī with ى, فِى.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا فَرَغَ الْأَسْعَدُ مِنْ شِعْرِهِ مَدَّ يَدَهُ عِنْدَ رَأْسِهِ فَوَجَدَ رَغِيفًا وَكُوزَ مَاءٍ مَالِحٍ فَأَكَلَ قَلِيلًا لِيَسُدَّ خَلَّتَهُ وَرَمَقَهُ وَشَرِبَ قَلِيلًا مِنَ الْمَاءِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā faragha al-Asʿadu min shiʿrihi madda yadahu ʿinda raʾsihi fa-wajada raghīfan wa-kūza māʾin māliḥin fa-akala qalīlan li-yasudda khallatahu wa-ramaqahu wa-shariba qalīlan mina al-māʾi
sentences.l: And-when finished al-Asʿad from his-verse, he-stretched-out his-hand by his-head and-found a-loaf and-a-jug (of) water salt; and-he-ate a-little to-stop-up his-want and-his-last-breath, and-drank a-little of the-water.
sentences.i: When al-Asʿad had finished his verses he reached out his hand beside his head and found a loaf and a jug of salt water. He ate a little, enough to stay his hunger and keep the life in him, and drank a little of the water.
sentences.n: faragha min, “to finish with”: min marks what is done. madda yadahu, “he stretched out his hand”; the shadda of مدّ is printed. The hamza of raʾs is not printed here, راسه, though it was in the night before. māʾ māliḥ, “salt water”, again with the later language's māliḥ for Classical milḥ. li-yasudda, “in order to stop up”: li- of purpose with the subjunctive; its shadda, ليسدّ, is printed. sadda al-ramaqa, “to stop up the last breath”, is a set phrase for eating just enough to stay alive: ramaq is the last remnant of life. khalla, “want, need”, is read here with a shadda the print does not show, the same idiom with a plainer word.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ يَزَلْ سَهْرَانًا إِلَى الصَّبَاحِ مِنْ كَثْرَهِ الْبَقِّ وَالْقَمْلِ
sentences.tr: wa-lam yazal sahrānan ilā al-ṣabāḥi min kathrati al-baqqi wa-al-qamli
sentences.l: And-not he-ceased wakeful until the-morning, from (the) abundance (of) the-bugs and-the-lice.
sentences.i: He lay awake until morning for the swarms of bugs and lice.
sentences.n: lam yazal, “he did not cease”, with an accusative predicate, “he stayed”. sahrānan, “wakeful”, has tanwīn: Classical Arabic treats adjectives of the pattern faʿlān as diptotes, sahrāna, but the later language gives them tanwīn, as the print does here with its alif. min of cause, “because of”. kathra, “abundance”, is spelled with ه for ة, كثره, as the print does now and then; it is kept and read kathrati. baqq, “bugs, gnats”: the shadda of البقّ and the fatḥa on the qāf of القَمْل, “lice”, are printed.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا أَصْبَحَ الصَّبَاحُ نَزَلَتْ إِلَيْهِ الْجَارِيَةُ وَغَيَّرَتْ أَثْوَابَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā aṣbaḥa al-ṣabāḥu nazalat ilayhi al-jāriyatu wa-ghayyarat athwābahu
sentences.l: And-when the-morning morninged, came-down to-him the-slave-girl and-changed his-garments.
sentences.i: When morning came the slave-girl came down to him and changed his clothes.
sentences.n: aṣbaḥa al-ṣabāḥu, “the morning dawned”, a stock phrase with verb and subject from the same root. ghayyara, Form II of gh-y-r, “to change”: she strips his old clothes off him. athwāb, plural of thawb, “garment”.

sentences.t: وَكَانَتْ قَدْ غُمِرَتْ بِالدَّمِ وَالْتَصَقَتْ عَلَى جِلْدِهِ فَطَلَعَ جِلْدُهُ مَعَ الْقَمِيصِ فَصَرَخَ وَتَأَوَّهَ
sentences.tr: wa-kānat qad ghumirat bi-al-dami wa-iltaṣaqat ʿalā jildihi fa-ṭalaʿa jilduhu maʿa al-qamīṣi fa-ṣarakha wa-taʾawwaha
sentences.l: And-they-had been-drowned with-the-blood and-stuck on his-skin, so-came-off his-skin with the-shirt, and-he-cried-out and-groaned.
sentences.i: They had been soaked in blood and had stuck to his skin, so that his skin came away with the shirt, and he cried out and groaned.
sentences.n: kānat qad ghumirat, “they had been soaked”: kāna with qad and a past verb makes a pluperfect, and the feminine singular agrees with athwāb, a broken plural of things. ghumira bi-, passive of ghamara, “to flood, cover over”: bi- marks what drenches them. iltaṣaqa, Form VIII of l-ṣ-q, “to stick, cling”; Classical Arabic says iltaṣaqa bi-, the print has ʿalā. ṭalaʿa, “to go up”, is used in the later language for “to come out, come off”. taʾawwaha, Form V of ʾ-w-h, “to say āh, to groan”; its shadda, تاوّه, is printed, but not the hamza.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ يَا مَوْلَايَ إِنْ كَانَ فِي هٰذَا رِضَاكَ فَزِدْنِي مِنْهُ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla yā mawlāya in kāna fī hādhā riḍāka fa-zidnī minhu
sentences.l: And-he-said: O my-master, if is in this your-good-pleasure, then-increase-me of-it.
sentences.i: And he said, “O my Lord, if Your good pleasure lies in this, then give me more of it.
sentences.n: yā mawlāya, “O my master”, is addressed to God. in kāna … fa-, “if … then”: the answer of the condition, an imperative, takes fa-. riḍā, “contentment, good pleasure”, is the subject of kāna, its case unseen in the final -ā. zāda, “to give more to”, imperative zid, with -nī, “me”: min marks what more is given of.

sentences.t: يَا رَبِّ إِنَّكَ لَسْتَ غَافِلًا عَمَّنْ ظَلَمَنِي فَخُذْ حَقِّي مِنْهُ
sentences.tr: yā rabbi innaka lasta ghāfilan ʿamman ẓalamanī fa-khudh ḥaqqī minhu
sentences.l: O my-Lord, indeed-you not-are heedless about-whoever wronged-me, so-take my-due from-him.
sentences.i: O Lord, You are not unmindful of the one who has wronged me: take from him what is owed me.”
sentences.n: yā rabbi, “O my Lord”, with the -ī of “my” shortened to -i, as usual in address; the shadda of ربّ is printed. lasta ghāfilan, “you are not heedless”: laysa takes its predicate in the accusative; ghafala ʿan, “to be heedless of”: ʿan marks what is overlooked, and ʿamman is ʿan + man, “of him who”. The words echo the Qurʾān, “do not think God heedless of what the wrongdoers do” (14:42). akhadha ḥaqqahu min, “to take one's due from”, to exact redress: min marks the one who owes it.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ صَعَّدَ الزَّفَرَاتِ وَأَنْشَدَ هٰذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ
sentences.tr: thumma ṣaʿʿada al-zafarāti wa-anshada hādhihi al-abyāta
sentences.l: Then he-sent-up the-sighs and-recited these verses:
sentences.i: Then he heaved deep sighs and recited these lines:

sentences.t:
صَبْرًا لِحُكْمِكَ يَا اِلَهِي فِى الْقَضَا * اَنَا صَابِرٌ اِنْ كَانَ فِيهِ لَكَ الرِّضَا
صَبْرًا لِمَا قَدَّرْتَهُ يَا سَيِّدِي * صَبْرًا وَلَوْ اُلْقِيتُ فِي نَارِ الْغَضَا
جَارُوْا عَلَيَّ بِظُلْمِهِمْ وَقَدِ اعْتَدَوْا * فَلَعَلَّ بِالْحَسَنَاتِ اَنْ تَتَعَوَّضَا
حَاشَاكَ تَغْفَلُ سَيِّدِي عَنْ ظَالِمٍ * فَوَسِيْلَتِي بِكَ اَنْتَ يَا رَبَّ الْقَضَا
sentences.tr:
ṣabran li-ḥukmika yā ilāhī fī al-qaḍā * anā ṣābirun in kāna fīhi laka al-riḍā
ṣabran li-mā qaddartahu yā sayyidī * ṣabran wa-law ulqītu fī nāri al-ghaḍā
jārū ʿalayya bi-ẓulmihim wa-qadi iʿtadaw * fa-laʿalla bi-al-ḥasanāti an tataʿawwaḍā
ḥāshāka taghfulu sayyidī ʿan ẓālimin * fa-wasīlatī bika anta yā rabba al-qaḍā
sentences.l:
Patience for your-judgement, O my-God, in the-decree! * I (am) patient, if is in-it for-you the-good-pleasure.
Patience for-what you-decreed-it, O my-master! * Patience, even-if I-were-cast in (the) fire (of) the-ghaḍā!
They-tyrannised over-me with-their-wrong and-have transgressed; * and-perhaps with-the-good-things that (it) be-recompensed.
Far-be-it-from-you (that) you-be-heedless, my-master, of a-wrongdoer! * And-my-means (is) in-you, you, O Lord (of) the-decree.
sentences.i:
Patience, my God, with Your judgement in what is fated! * I am patient, if in this Your pleasure lies.
Patience with what You have ordained, my Master, * patience, though I were thrown into the fire of the ghaḍā!
They have wronged me and oppressed me and gone too far; * perhaps it will all be made good to me in blessings.
Far be it from You, my Master, to overlook a wrongdoer! * You alone are my recourse, O Lord of fate.
sentences.n: Four lines in the metre kāmil, rhyming in -ḍā. The print points the verse fully. ṣabran, “patience!”, an accusative verbal noun standing for a whole sentence, “I will be patient”; li- marks what it is shown towards. al-qaḍā, “the decree, what is fated”, is qaḍāʾ with its hamza dropped at the rhyme, as the print spells it in both lines that end with it; al-riḍā and al-ghaḍā rhyme with it. The metre wants anā, “I”, read short, ana. ghaḍā is a desert tree whose wood burns long and fiercely, so that “the fire of the ghaḍā” is proverbial for a hard and lasting fire. law, “even if”, with ulqītu, passive of alqā, Form IV of l-q-y, “to throw”. jāra ʿalā, “to act tyrannously towards”: ʿalā marks the victim; iʿtadā, Form VIII of ʿ-d-w, “to transgress”. fa-laʿalla … an tataʿawwaḍā is loose: laʿalla, “perhaps”, has no noun after it and is followed, like ʿasā, by an with the subjunctive; taʿawwaḍa, Form V of ʿ-w-ḍ, “to receive in exchange”, and the -ā is the subjunctive's -a lengthened at the rhyme. tataʿawwaḍā may be “you are recompensed”, the poet speaking to himself, or “it”, his soul, “is recompensed”; either way the sense is that good will come in return. bi- marks what is received in exchange. ḥāshāka, “far be it from You”, is followed directly by the imperfect, taghfulu, where Classical Arabic would want ḥāshāka an taghfula. wasīla, “means of approach”, the intercession one brings to a patron: bika anta, “in You, You Yourself”, makes God both the patron and the means. The print writes the hamza-bearing alifs bare, as in اِلَهِي, اَنَا, اُلْقِيتُ and اَنْتَ, and writes ilāhī, “my God”, without any sign of its long ā, اِلَهِي, where it uses the dagger alif elsewhere. It sets a sukūn on the wāw of جَارُوْا and on the yāʾ of وَسِيْلَتِي, marks a long vowel does not need. fī is spelled with ى, فِى, in line 1 and with ي, فِي, in line 2.

sentences.i: And the words of another poet:
sentences.n: A heading, as in the anthologies: “and the saying of another”, a second poem on the same theme. The madda of الآخر is printed.

sentences.t:
كُنْ عَنْ اُمُوْرِكَ مُعْرِضَا * وَكِلِ الْاُمُوْرَ اِلَى الْقَضَا
فَلَرُبَّ اَمْرٍ مُسْخِطٍ * لَكَ فِي عَوَاقِبِهِ رِضَى
وَلَرُبَّمَا اتَّسَعَ الْمَضِيْقُ * وَرَبُّمَا ضَاقَ الْفَضَا
اَللّٰهُ يَفْعَلُ مَا يَشَاءُ * فَلَا تَكُنْ مُتَعَرِّضَا
وَابْشِرْ بِخَيْرٍ عَاجِلٍ * تَنْسَى بِهِ مَاقَدْ مَضَى
sentences.tr:
kun ʿan umūrika muʿriḍā * wa-kili al-umūra ilā al-qaḍā
fa-la-rubba amrin muskhiṭin * laka fī ʿawāqibihi riḍā
wa-la-rubbamā ittasaʿa al-maḍīqu * wa-rubbamā ḍāqa al-faḍā
Allāhu yafʿalu mā yashāʾu * fa-lā takun mutaʿarriḍā
wa-bshir bi-khayrin ʿājilin * tansā bihi mā qad maḍā
sentences.l:
Be about your-affairs turning-away, * and-entrust the-affairs to the-decree.
For-many-a matter displeasing * to-you, in its-outcomes (is) contentment.
And-often has-grown-wide the-narrow-place, * and-often has-grown-narrow the-open-space.
God does what he-wills, * so-do-not be opposing.
And-rejoice in-a-good soon-coming, * you-forget by-it what has passed.
sentences.i:
Turn your mind from your troubles, * and leave all things to fate.
For many a thing that grieves you * holds contentment in its end.
Often the narrow strait grows wide, * and often the open plain grows close.
God does as He wills, * so do not set yourself against Him.
Take heart, good will come soon, * and you will forget all that is past.
sentences.n: Five lines in the short form of the metre kāmil, rhyming in -ḍā. The print points the verse fully. muʿriḍ ʿan, Form IV of ʿ-r-ḍ, “turning away from”: ʿan marks what is left aside; muʿriḍā is the accusative muʿriḍan, held in pause at the rhyme. kili, imperative of wakala ilā, “to entrust to”: ilā marks the one trusted. rubba, “many a”, takes an indefinite noun in the genitive, here with la- of emphasis; muskhiṭ, active participle of Form IV of s-kh-ṭ, “that angers, displeases”. riḍā, spelled here with ى, رِضَى, and with alif, الرِّضَا, in the poem before. rubbamā, “often, it may be”. In line 3 the print sets the second rubbamā as وَرَبُّمَا, with a fatḥa on the rāʾ and a damma on the bāʾ, where the first is correctly وَلَرُبَّمَا; the word can only be rubbamā, and it is read so here, the printed marks kept in the Arabic, while the transliteration gives the intended rubbamā. ittasaʿa, Form VIII of w-s-ʿ, “to grow wide”, against ḍāqa, “to grow narrow”: maḍīq, “a strait, a narrow pass”, and faḍāʾ, “open country”, here faḍā without its hamza at the rhyme. The first halves of lines 3 and 4 run one syllable long as printed; the extra syllable falls away if al-maḍīqu and yashāʾu are read in pause, al-maḍīq and yashāʾ. mutaʿarriḍ, Form V of ʿ-r-ḍ, “one who sets himself against, interferes”. The print leaves the alif of وَابْشِرْ bare and unmarked, so that it joins on as wa-bshir; the word is abshir, Form IV of b-sh-r, “rejoice!”, whose hamza is dropped for the metre. abshir bi-: bi- marks the good news. ʿājil, “coming soon, swift”. tansā bihi, “you will forget by it”: bi- of cause. The print runs mā and qad together, مَاقَدْ, and that is kept. It writes the hamza-bearing alifs bare, as in اُمُوْرِكَ, اِلَى and اَمْرٍ, and points Allāh in full with its dagger alif, اَللّٰهُ; it sets a sukūn on the wāw of اُمُوْرِكَ and الْاُمُوْرَ and on the yāʾ of الْمَضِيْقُ, marks a long vowel does not need.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا فَرَغَ مِنْ شِعْرِهِ نَزَلَتْ عَلَيْهِ الْجَارِيَةُ بِالضَّرْبِ حَتَّى غُشِيَ عَلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā faragha min shiʿrihi nazalat ʿalayhi al-jāriyatu bi-al-ḍarbi ḥattā ghushiya ʿalayhi
sentences.l: And-when he-finished from his-verse, came-down upon-him the-slave-girl with-the-beating until it-was-covered over-him.
sentences.i: When he had finished his verses the slave-girl came down on him with blows until he fainted.
sentences.n: nazala ʿalā … bi-, “to come down on someone with”, to set about him: bi- marks what she brings. ghushiya ʿalayhi, “he fainted”, literally “it was covered over him”, an impersonal passive with ʿalā marking the one who swoons; this is the Classical form, where the night before the print had ghumiya ʿalayhi.

sentences.t: وَرَمَتْ لَهُ رَغِيفًا وَكُوزَمَاءٍ مَالِحٍ وَطَلَعَتْ مِنْ عِنْدِهِ وَخَلَّتْهُ وَحِيدًا فَرِيدًا حَزِينًا
sentences.tr: wa-ramat lahu raghīfan wa-kūza māʾin māliḥin wa-ṭalaʿat min ʿindihi wa-khallathu waḥīdan farīdan ḥazīnan
sentences.l: And-she-threw to-him a-loaf and-a-jug-(of)-water salt, and-went-up from with-him, and-left-him alone, solitary, sorrowful.
sentences.i: She threw him a loaf and a jug of salt water, and went up and away from him, leaving him alone, forsaken and grieving.
sentences.n: ramā li-, “to throw to”: li- marks the one it is thrown to. The print again runs كوز ماء, “a jug of water”, together as كوزماء, and that is kept. ṭalaʿa min ʿindihi, “she went up from his presence”: he lies in a hall under the ground, and ṭalaʿa, “to go up”, is also the later language's “to go out”. khallā, Form II of kh-l-w, “to leave”; its shadda, خلّته, is printed. waḥīdan farīdan ḥazīnan, three accusatives of state, “alone, solitary, sorrowful”, the first two near-synonyms paired by rhyme.

sentences.t: وَالدِّمَاءُ تَسِيلُ مِنْ أَجْنَابِهِ وَهُوَ مُقَيَّدٌ فِى الْحَدِيدِ بَعِيدٌ عَنِ الْأَحْبَابِ
sentences.tr: wa-al-dimāʾu tasīlu min ajnābihi wa-huwa muqayyadun fī al-ḥadīdi baʿīdun ʿani al-aḥbābi
sentences.l: And-the-bloods flowing from his-sides, and-he (was) fettered in the-iron, far from the-loved-ones.
sentences.i: The blood was running from his sides, and he lay fettered in irons, far from those he loved.
sentences.n: wa- here opens two circumstantial clauses, “while the blood ran … and he was fettered …”. dimāʾ, plural of dam, “blood”, for blood that flows; ajnāb, plural of janb, “side, flank”. al-ḥadīd, “iron”, means fetters. muqayyadun and baʿīdun are both predicates of huwa. The sajʿ falls on ajnābihi / al-aḥbābi, with an inner chime in al-ḥadīd / baʿīd. The shadda of مقيّد is printed, and fī is spelled with ى, فى.

sentences.t: فَبَكَى وَتَذَكَّرَ أَخَاهُ وَالْعِزَّ الَّذِي كَانَ فِيهِ
sentences.tr: fa-bakā wa-tadhakkara akhāhu wa-al-ʿizza alladhī kāna fīhi
sentences.l: And-he-wept, and-remembered his-brother and-the-might which he-was in-it.
sentences.i: He wept, and thought of his brother and of the glory he had once known.
sentences.n: akhāhu, “his brother”, accusative: akh is one of the nouns that lengthen their case vowel before a suffix, akhūhu, akhāhu, akhīhi. The shadda of تذكّر and of العزّ is printed.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the-morning overtook Shahrazād, and-she-fell-silent from the-permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The closing formula, as at the end of every night. The rhyme falls on al-ṣabāḥ / al-mubāḥ.
